_note: Narration script for the Asthma module (CPP-050-AO v3.1). Lee on eleven_v4, one take, short conversational sentences. Captions use the text here; the prompt starts with [calmly] and spells initialisms out (see tools/video/voice.json).

lines.head: Introduction
sentences: Asthma.
What every Ambulance Officer needs to know.

lines.head: The key idea
sentences: Asthma treatment is all about relieving bronchospasm, with bronchodilators.
Start with basic care. Then use the Asthma Severity and Treatment Table to guide you.

lines.head: Allergy first
sentences: Could this be allergy, or anaphylaxis? Think about it every time.
If it is, follow the anaphylaxis protocol first. That includes early clinical support.

lines.head: Judge the severity
sentences: Mild asthma? They talk in full sentences, with a normal work of breathing.
More severe? Only phrases, or words, or they can't speak. And they're distressed.
Life threatening? Unable to speak. Drowsy or unconscious. Cyanosed, with poor breathing effort.
And never judge severity on the oxygen saturation alone.

lines.head: Mild asthma
sentences: For mild asthma, follow their own asthma plan, if that's appropriate.
Or give salbutamol through an MDI and spacer. One puff is 100 micrograms.
That's 12 puffs if they're 6 or older. Or 6 puffs from 1 to 6 years.

lines.head: No spacer
sentences: Can't manage the spacer? If they're under 4, consider adding a resuscitation mask.
Or nebulise salbutamol. 2.5 milligrams from 1 to 6 years, made up to 5 mL with saline.
And 5 milligrams if they're over 6.

lines.head: Not improving
sentences: Not improving after salbutamol? Consult the EOC Clinician. They may advise repeat doses.
Consider clinical support, keep up basic care, and transport.

lines.head: More severe
sentences: More severe asthma? Request clinical support early.
Start nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium. Over 6, that's 5 milligrams and 500 micrograms.
From 1 to 6, it's 2.5 milligrams and 250 micrograms, with 3 mL of saline to make 5 mL.

lines.head: Life threatening
sentences: Life threatening? High flow oxygen, and early clinical support.
If you need to ventilate with the bag valve mask, keep it small, slow and gentle. That lets the chest deflate.
The EOC Clinician may advise continuous salbutamol, or IM adrenaline. Then it's urgent transport.

lines.head: Getting worse
sentences: If they get worse at any point, consult the EOC Clinician straight away.
And if they become unresponsive and aren't breathing normally, start CPR.

lines.head: Wrap-up
sentences: So. Think anaphylaxis.
Judge the severity.
Spacer for mild.
Nebs and early support for more severe.
And call the EOC Clinician early.
Now, have a go with the asthma checker on this page.
